title: Regional Transit Node Architecture: GLMZ's Connections to the Outside
body:
GLMZ is not an island, though it sometimes functions as though it were. The megacity maintains five Regional Transit Nodes — major infrastructure complexes that connect the city's internal transit network to inter-city rail, regional road freight corridors, and the Great Lakes water transit system. These nodes are: Meridian North Station (Velorant-operated, primary passenger rail), Meridian South Freight Terminal (Caldor-operated, road and rail freight), Portsmith Water Transit Hub (jointly operated under a Harmon-Caldor compact, lake freighter and passenger ferry), East Industrial Gateway (Sable-operated, specialized corporate logistics), and the contested Meridian West Interchange, currently under a three-way ownership dispute that has delayed a major expansion for six years.

Meridian North Station is the face the city presents to the outside world, and it is a face carefully composed for a specific audience. The station's main concourse — a vaulted space of considerable architectural ambition, rebuilt in 2158 — is calibrated for the experience of arriving and departing Tier-One and Tier-Two passengers. Immigration and identity verification for arriving travelers from other city-states and autonomous zones is handled at Tier-One-speed gates with biometric neural scanning; holders of foreign citizenship-equivalent credentials from recognized corporate sovereigns pass in under two minutes. Travelers from non-recognized jurisdictions — including several of the independent communities in the northern lake basin — face a secondary processing track that can take hours and includes mandatory data-device inspection. The distinction is less about security than about establishing legibility within the corporate identity architecture.

The Portsmith Water Transit Hub serves a function often overlooked in analyses of the city's transit infrastructure: it is the primary physical connection between GLMZ and the lake basin communities that exist outside corporate sovereignty structures. Fishing cooperatives, independent settlements, and the loose network of water-traveling communities that have developed in the post-consolidation era all interface with the megacity primarily through Portsmith. The Hub's commercial freight docks handle an enormous volume of food imports — approximately 18 percent of the city's fresh food supply moves through Portsmith on lake freighters. The passenger ferry terminals are smaller and notably less surveilled than the rail nodes, a fact not lost on people whose movement between the city and the outside world benefits from reduced scrutiny.

Regional transit nodes are also sites of significant informal economic activity and, periodically, of political consequence. The zones immediately adjacent to the freight terminals — particularly around South Terminal and East Gateway — have developed dense informal economies of fixers, brokers, and logistics intermediaries who manage the gap between formal corporate freight systems and the needs of smaller operators, unlicensed businesses, and individuals moving goods that do not fit comfortably within the sanctioned logistics architecture. MSA maintains permanent checkpoint stations at all five nodes, but the volume of traffic — particularly freight — makes comprehensive inspection impossible, a fact that the informal economy has structured itself around with considerable sophistication.
